imageCaption: Elijah and Marco lean over a domino table in the street, the neighborhood gathered in evening light; Sully lies nearby watching with absolute attention; yellow buildings frame the scene.
text:
The domino table was already set up on the street by 4:00 PM, which meant the neighborhood had either been very optimistic or very confident. Aaliyah was starting to suspect it was the latter.

She watched from the yellow doorway as Anthony and Luisana ventured into the street with their contribution—a massive batch of Anthony's arroz con pollo that Luisana had supervised but which carried the unmistakable stamp of Anthony's philosophy, which was "more" applied to every ingredient except "subtlety." The dish smelled like it could start its own economy.

"This is going to be good," Elijah said, appearing beside her with the kind of certainty usually reserved for things he'd already eaten multiple times.

"You've never been to a neighborhood domino tournament," Aaliyah pointed out.

"No," Elijah agreed. "But I've seen dominoes. I understand the stakes. There are numbers. There's strategy. There's the possibility of someone getting very emotionally invested in a game piece. All of those things are extremely good."

He wasn't wrong. By 5:15 PM, the street had transformed into something that suggested the neighborhood had been waiting for this specific Saturday for precisely seventy-four days. There were tables, music from at least two sources, lanterns being hung between buildings even though the sun wouldn't set for hours. There were children. There were people of every age Aaliyah could identify, and some ages she'd never actually seen exist before.

And at the center of everything was Marco, who was apparently the de facto keeper of tournament rules and had opinions about hand placement, tile positioning, and the proper psychological approach to a domino match.

"You," Marco said, pointing directly at Elijah like he was an expert scout who'd identified tremendous potential in an unexpected location. "You play?"

"I don't think so," Elijah said. "But I think I want to learn."

This appeared to be exactly the correct response. Marco pulled out a chair, handed Elijah a set of tiles, and began explaining the rules in a way that involved using his hands to demonstrate geometry, fortune, and the delicate balance between planning and hope.

Sully had claimed a spot directly under the table—not underneath in the way of a dog begging for scraps, but underneath in the way of a dog who understood that he was security for something very important happening above his head. He watched the dominoes with the kind of attention usually reserved for birds.

"He thinks he's a referee," Rosa said, appearing at Aaliyah's elbow with a plate of something that smelled like history and care. "The dog always knows when dominoes matter. Last month, my cousin brought her new puppy to the tournament, and it was very confused. Your dog understands the ritual."

Aaliyah took the plate—some kind of stewed meat with bread—and realized she was being fed as a form of neighborhood integration. "Sully's good at understanding things that are important. I don't know how he does it."

"Presence," Rosa said simply. "The dog has presence. You can tell by the way he's listening. Presence is rare. It's why your family's house was waiting for your family. The house knew you would have presence."

Which was, Aaliyah would later realize, the exact kind of thing that sounded strange if you analyzed it too carefully, but which made perfect sense if you understood that some neighborhoods operated on frequency rather than fact.

By 6:00 PM, Elijah had played his first game and lost in exactly the way a person loses when they're playing against someone who's been perfecting domino strategy for sixty-seven years. Marco shook his hand like this was significant—like losing to him was a kind of credential.

"You have the right energy," Marco announced to no one in particular and therefore to everyone. "You make moves that feel lucky instead of safe. This is how dominoes should be played. With feeling."

Anthony, having circled back to the table with Luisana, heard this and raised his eyebrows at Aaliyah in a way that clearly communicated: *the dog barks, the boy plays dominoes, the universe organizes itself around feeling—this man understands our entire life philosophy.*

But then something shifted.

It wasn't visible, exactly. Aaliyah would have trouble explaining it to Aaliyah-from-three-days-ago. But it was the kind of shift that Sully noticed first—his ears came up, his tail stopped wagging, and he produced three quick barks that Elijah had taught the family to recognize.

Minor glitch nearby.

The dominoes trembled. Just barely. Just enough that if you weren't paying attention, you'd think someone had walked past the table. But Aaliyah was paying attention, and she understood that the thing walking past wasn't a person.

It was a moment trying to occupy the same space twice.

"Marco," Rosa said calmly, "is the domino set from 1987 or 2023?"

"Both," Marco said, equally calmly, like this was a normal question to field during a tournament. "The set belonged to my father. When he died, I bought a new one that was identical. Sometimes they don't know which set they should be. Dominoes remember who played them."

The tiles stilled. One set solidified—the newer one, Aaliyah could tell, because it smelled less like memory and more like manufacture. The other set seemed to fade, not completely but enough that it wasn't there anymore. Or rather, it was there in a time where people still knew how to play 1987 games.

"That happens once or twice a month," Rosa said to Aaliyah's expression of relative panic. "Ever since the Cascade started. Marco just plays both sets until one of them remembers which timeline it lives in. Last week we had a tournament where dominoes were playing themselves. Very aggressive strategy. Marco's father won, which was nice. He's been dead four years."

"Right," Aaliyah said faintly. "Okay. That's... I'm going to need to sit down."

But she didn't sit. Instead, she found herself walking closer to the table, to the dominoes that were still slightly trembling, and she understood with the part of her brain that had been mapping glitches for seventy-four days that this wasn't a dangerous moment.

This was a nostalgic moment. This was a neighborhood remembering itself. This was dominoes trying to figure out which version of their story they were supposed to tell.

"Can I ask," she said to Marco, "why the glitch is still happening if we're here? If family emotional resonance is supposed to stabilize things?"

Marco considered this while placing another domino with the kind of care usually reserved for heart surgery.

"Because," he said finally, "the Cascade doesn't know you're supposed to stay yet. You've only been in the yellow house for two days. The street is still telling the universe that you're visiting. The dominoes are confused about the timeline because the neighborhood is confused about whether you belong."

He looked up at her directly. His expression was kind but not soft—it was the expression of someone telling the absolute truth without making it prettier than it needed to be.

"Saturday," he said, "you need to cook something that proves you're staying. Not tomorrow. Saturday. The street party. You need to bring your family's food and share it the way people do who plan to be here next season."

Aaliyah felt the weight of that suddenly. Not the weight of commitment—she'd made that decision already. But the weight of ceremony. Of stepping into a neighborhood's expectations and understanding that sometimes you stabilize glitches not by existing, but by making promises.

"Okay," she said. "We'll be ready."

Marco smiled. And on the street in Willemstad, with dominoes sorting themselves between timelines and a dog standing guard, something shifted back to solid.

The neighborhood was still confused about whether the Gomez family belonged.

But it was definitely paying attention now.
